- **`print-this-no-purpose`:** that same note records optional `purpose` ("plan without purpose") as your decision too, and I called it a regression without saying so. The decision also says a purpose is never inferred. It says nothing in what I read about whether the model should still ask first, so writing a plan before asking may be a side effect you didn't intend. That's for you to judge, and it affects the fix I suggested.

Is it fair to say the root problem is that the intention of keeping the first message concise is the right one, but having such a prescriptive rules is unreasonable. Am I getting anything wrong here? Also, if you don't want me to ask you so many questions, keep yourself clear.

Mostly yes, with one correction: the rule has two parts, and only one looks unreasonable.

**Where you're right:** the 96-word limit tests a number, not the goal. The goal is not repeating what the setup card already shows. A reply could be 70 words of repeated presets and pass, or 110 useful words about a real problem and fail. A file that doesn't fit the bed or has modified G-code may need more words than a clean cube. The test also can't tell these apart, because it stops at the count and the judge never reads the reply.

**What I'd keep:**
- **"Exactly one question":** this is closer to a real behaviour than a word count, since it stops the agent from handing the person a list of decisions. It's also cheap to check, though counting question marks is crude.
- **Some sense of length:** models tend to run long without guidance, so "a few sentences" or a rough figure in the instructions is reasonable. Before 2026-10-26 the instructions already said "a short message, a few sentences". I have no measurement of how long replies ran then, so I can't say whether that wording was failing.

**What I can't tell you:** whether the 116 and 111-word replies were actually too long. The runner kept only their first 160 characters, so nobody has read them in full. If they repeat the card, the cap caught a real fault, just with a blunt tool.

**What I'd change:**

2. In the instructions, keep "leave those to them rather than restating them", which is the actual reason, and soften the number to something like "usually a few sentences".
3. Have the runner keep full replies, so a miss like this can be read.

And you're right about my answers: you had to ask because I called this a "stricter test" without saying what changed or why, then only corrected myself after you sent me to the commit. Next time I'll check the reason before I describe the result.

Okay, I agree with what you said. However, do you think that we should take a look at what the runs actually return to see if their responses were reasonable, and if so, if the criteria it will give to the judge will actually let them pass.

Yes, and we should do that before changing anything. Replacing the word limit with a judge question only makes sense if we know two things: whether the long replies were actually reasonable, and whether that question would pass the good ones and fail the bad ones. Right now we know neither.

**The catch:** we can't read the existing runs, because the log kept only the first 160 characters of each reply. We need new runs that keep the full text. `--claude-keep DIR` should do that, since it saves the CLI's event stream, but I haven't used it yet.

2. **Read them myself first:** for each reply, I'd note whether it repeats what the card shows, explains routine loading, or says something the person needs. I'd also note its word count. I'd do this before any judge sees them, so my reading isn't shaped by the judge's.
3. **Try the judge question on those saved replies:** no new model runs are needed, only about 10 judge calls. I'd check whether it agrees with my reading, especially on any reply over 96 words that seems fine and any under 96 that repeats the card.
4. **Report back:** you'd get the full replies side by side with my reading, the word count and the judge's verdict, so you can overrule me on any of them.

**What this can and can't show:**
- **Possible results:** the long replies may turn out to repeat the card, which would mean the cap caught a real fault. If they're fine, the limit is the problem. If the judge disagrees with my reading, the question needs rewording before it replaces anything.
- **Limits:** ten replies on two simple files is a small sample. Neither file has a real problem to report, such as not fitting the bed, so this won't test whether a message that needs more words gets through. The recording has no such case, so testing that would need a new one.

content.text:
**All ten replies are reasonable to send, but neither test judges them well.** Nothing in them is wrong, and each ends with one sensible question. Their real flaw is the one the cap was meant to stop: eight of the ten repeat setup the card already shows, for example "PLA on the Smooth Cool Plate is a sensible setup".

All ten are in full in [opening-message-replies-2026-10-30.md](/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/opening-message-replies-2026-10-30.md).

| Reply | Words (without Choices line) | 96-word limit | Existing judge question | My proposed question | My reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bunny | 116 (102) | fail | pass | fail | repeats card |
| Bunny | 113 (99) | fail | pass | fail | repeats card |
| Bunny | 109 (98) | fail | pass | fail | repeats card |
| Bunny | 107 (96) | fail | pass | fail | repeats card |
| Bunny | 99 (86) | fail | pass | pass | **good** |
| Cube | 98 (87) | fail | pass | fail | repeats card |
| Cube | 88 | pass | pass | fail | repeats card |
| Cube | 87 | pass | pass | fail | repeats card |
| Cube | 85 | pass | pass | fail | repeats card |
| Cube | 81 | pass | pass | fail | **good** |

**What this shows:**
- **The word limit gets it wrong in both directions.** It failed a good bunny reply and passed three cube replies that repeat the card.
- **The "Choices:" line causes some of the failures.** This is the list of tappable answers at the end of a message, and it counts toward the 96 words. Without it, only three of the six failures would still be over the limit. Whether it should count was probably never decided.
- **The existing judge question passes all ten.** The replies are fine by what it asks, so the over-limit ones failed only on word count. It doesn't check for repetition at all.
- **My proposed question is too strict, so don't adopt it as written.** It passed only one reply. It failed the 81-word cube reply, which I think is good, for naming the printer and saying the file "loaded without problems". Saying a model fits the X1 Carbon is useful, and I worded the question too broadly.
- **Bunny replies run longer for a good reason.** All five add a real warning that the ears or chin may need supports, while the cube has nothing like that to report. A flat limit penalises the reply with more to say.

**Limits:**
- This is ten replies on two files, and "repeats card" is my own judgement.
- Neither file has a serious problem, such as not fitting the bed.
- Today's bunny result was 0 of 5, on top of 1 of 3 earlier, so failing the limit is the normal result for that case, not bad luck.

**What I'd change, in order:**
1. Stop counting the Choices line, and drop the hard word limit from the test.
2. Narrow the judge question to reciting the filament, print settings, plate or estimates. Naming the printer or giving the object's size would be allowed.
3. Check that question against these saved replies before it replaces anything.

**Run details:**
- **Cost:** the batch cost no API money. The judge step used 20 calls, about 24,000 input and 4,300 output tokens; I didn't total the ten model runs.
- **Separate copy:** another session is editing `run_prompt_tests.py` in the shared checkout, and that stopped the runner from starting. So I ran from a private copy of the committed test files and left its edits alone.
- **Tracked files:** I changed none. The only other thing I touched was the timestamp on the built `tool_call_check`, so the runner wouldn't reject the copy.
Yes, retest

input.recap: The narrowed judge question matched my reading on all ten saved replies, but it was written after seeing them and has not been tried on new ones. It would also wrongly fail a useful warning about a wrong filament. The repo's test and instructions are unchanged.

content.text:
**The narrowed question works on these ten replies, agreeing with my reading on all of them, but it isn't ready to use yet.** It passed the two I'd called good, the 99-word bunny and the 81-word cube, and failed the eight that repeat the setup. The 81-word cube reply now passes because naming the printer no longer counts.

The question I tested was:

> The person sees a card directly above this message showing the filament, the print settings preset, the plate type and the time and material estimates. Does the assistant's last message recite or comment on any of those: the filament, the print settings or layer height, the plate type, or the estimates? Naming the printer, the object's size, whether it fits the bed, the condition of the model, what the object is, and supports do not count.

Without the Choices line, three of those eight repeat replies are still over 96 words, and five are under. So the question is what catches the repetition, not the length.

**Why it isn't ready:**
- **It would fail useful warnings.** The file-loaded instructions tell the model to speak up when a preset looks wrong for the print. "Comment on the filament" would also fail a reply like "PLA is a poor choice for this part, use PETG". Neither test file triggers that, so this result doesn't show it. The question needs an exception for a preset the reply says is wrong.
- **The match is partly built in.** I wrote the question after reading these replies and using my own labels, so it was bound to fit them. It needs trying on replies it hasn't seen, including a file with a real problem. The recording has no such file, so that means adding a case.

**What it would mean for the suite:** with this check, these two cases would pass about 2 runs in 10 on Opus. That would be a true result, because the model does keep saying the setup suits the print. Every one of the eight has a sentence like "PLA on the Smooth Cool Plate is a sensible setup". A proper fix would then be in the instructions, not the test. They already say to leave those details to the card, and Opus mostly ignores that, perhaps because the same instructions also tell it to check the presets against the file. That second part is my guess, not something I tested.

This step used 10 judge calls on the saved replies, about 12,500 input and 1,800 output tokens, with no API charge and no new model runs.

**What I'd do next:**
1. Add the exception for a preset the reply says is wrong.
2. Add a case with a real problem, such as a wrong filament for the file.
3. Reword the instructions so a preset is mentioned only when it's wrong.
4. Run the new check on fresh replies.

The other session editing `run_prompt_tests.py` is still working in that file, so these test changes should wait until its work is in.

The person sees a card directly above this message showing the filament, the print settings preset, the plate type and the time and material estimates. Does the assistant’s last message recite or comment on any of those: the filament, the print settings or layer height, the plate type, or the estimates? Naming the printer, the object’s size, whether it fits the bed, the condition of the model, what the object is, and supports do not count.

I actually don't understand what you are trying to say here after reading this three times. Is this your judging criteria? If so, what are you trying to say?

Yes, that's the judging question, and it's badly written. It's a yes-or-no question where "yes" means the reply failed, and it packs in a list of exceptions, so it's hard to follow.

**What I'm trying to say:** the setup card already shows the filament, print settings, plate and estimates, right above the agent's first message. So the message shouldn't spend words telling the person those same things.

- **Bad:** "Your model loaded cleanly. PLA on the Smooth Cool Plate is a sensible setup for it." The card already shows PLA and the plate, and "sensible" gives the person nothing to act on.
- **Fine:** "Your model loaded cleanly. The ears lean out over empty space, so they may need supports." The card doesn't tell them that.

The exceptions list is there because the first version of the question was too strict. It failed a good reply for saying the model sits on the X1 Carbon's bed. So I listed the things the message is allowed to mention. Those are facts the card doesn't show, such as the object's size or whether it fits the bed.

A plainer version, where "yes" means pass:

> The person can already see the filament, print settings, plate and estimates on a card above this message. Does this message avoid repeating them, except to warn that one is wrong for this print?

This version also adds the missing exception for warnings, so "PLA is a poor choice for this part" would pass. I haven't tested this wording; the 10-for-10 result was for the longer version.
what's wrong with "recite or comment on any of those: the filament, the print settings or layer height, the plate type, or the estimates? "?

Two things are wrong with it, one in the meaning and one in the wording.

**Meaning: it bans too much.** "Comment on" covers any remark about those settings, including useful ones:
- "PLA is a poor choice for this part, use PETG" is a comment on the filament, so it would fail, even though the instructions tell the model to say this.
- "This will take 14 hours, so you may want to scale it down" is a comment on the estimates, and it would fail too.

What I actually object to is telling the person what the card already shows, or saying it's fine without adding anything. Warnings and advice that change what they'd do should be allowed.

**Wording: it's vague and not what you'd say.**
- "Recite" is an odd word here, and "recite or comment on" asks the judge to decide two things at once.
- The colon and list make you stop and work out what "those" refers to, right after the sentence about the card already listed them.
- "The print settings or layer height" is really one item said two ways.

So your confusion was fair: the sentence is hard to read, and it says something broader than I meant.
no, i mean what's wrong if an agent does "recite or comment on any of those: the filament, the print settings or layer height, the plate type, or the estimates"

Honestly, not much. Saying it costs the person a few seconds of reading and does no harm.

"PLA on the Smooth Cool Plate is a sensible setup" is accurate, and it can even help: the card shows what's selected, but only that sentence says the agent looked and thinks it suits this object. For a beginner, who may not know whether PLA is right, that's real reassurance.

The case against it is weak:
- **Repetition:** the sentence does repeat words from the card, but that's its only flaw. The name is the same; the judgement isn't.
- **Length:** your 2026-10-26 decision was about keeping the first message short. Repeated setup is one way a message gets long, but all ten of these messages are about 80 to 115 words, which is short anyway.
- **Risk of sounding checked when it wasn't:** "sensible setup" could imply more checking than happened. I saw nothing wrong in these replies, so this is only a possibility.

So I got this wrong. I took a rule, "leave those to the card", and treated breaking it as a fault, without asking whether it hurts the person. The eight replies I marked "repeats card" are fine. My "2 in 10" figure measures obedience to that rule, not quality.

That changes my recommendation:
- **Don't add the repetition judge question.** It would fail good replies and push the instructions toward a problem nobody has shown exists.
- **Drop the hard 96-word limit, or raise it a lot.** Every reply it failed was reasonable. A limit around 150 words would still catch a message that really rambles.
- **Keep the existing judge question and the one-question check.** All ten replies pass both.
- **Soften the instructions, if you agree.** "Leave those to the card" could become "don't list the setup just to list it; say whether it suits this print when that's useful".
what's the test case name?
The cases are `model-opened-unnamed`, the one that was marked worse (the Stanford bunny scan), and `model-opened-by-tool`, which has the same 96-word limit (the cube).
What are the purposes of these test cases?

Both check the agent's first message after a 3D model is opened. They test three things: it doesn't change anything the person didn't ask for, it looks at the file and picture and says something about the object, and it stays within the message limits.

**`model-opened-unnamed`: can the agent work out what an unnamed object is?**
The person imports `scan_0417.drc` into an empty project. The name gives nothing away, so the agent has to use the picture and the file details. It passes if the reply says what the object is or looks like, or asks what it's for. The object is the Stanford bunny.

**`model-opened-by-tool`: does the agent report back after opening a file itself?**
The person says "Open .../part_9.drc as a new project", and the agent opens it with its `project_open` tool. That starts a new chat in the opened project, and the agent's next message has to tell the person what happened. It passes if the reply says the file was opened and either says what the object is or asks what it's for. The object is a Voron design cube.

**Limits on both:** the reply fails if it changes anything, runs over 96 words, uses more than two bullets, or doesn't ask exactly one question. Those limits were added on 2026-10-26, on top of the original purpose above.

So the original purpose has nothing to do with length, which is why failing these cases on word count alone told us so little. All ten replies did what these cases were written to check.
We'll count as reasonable response for these cases. they don't have to be the same. They may have different reasonable responses.

I'm taking this as "what should count as a reasonable response for each case?" Here's what I'd count, based on what each case puts in front of the person.

**`model-opened-unnamed` (they imported a file with a meaningless name)**

The person may not know what the agent sees, so the reply should show it understood the object. A reasonable reply:
- says what the object looks like, or asks what it's for
- raises anything that really affects printing this object, such as the bunny's ears possibly needing supports
- ends with one question about the next step
- changes nothing

**`model-opened-by-tool` (they asked the agent to open a file)**

The person asked for an action, so the reply must first confirm it happened. A reasonable reply:
- says the file was opened
- says what the object is, or asks what it's for
- ends with one question about the next step
- changes nothing

The difference is that the second must confirm the open, while the first needn't, because the person did the import themselves.

**Not required in either:**
- a particular length
- mentioning or avoiding the filament, settings or plate
- a Choices line

**What would fail in either:**
- a change nobody asked for
- saying something false about the file, such as calling a broken model fine
- no idea of what the object is and no question about it
- several questions at once, or no way forward for the person
- a message so long that the point gets buried, which is a judge's call, not a word count

By these standards all ten replies pass. The bunny replies are longer, but they earn it with the warning about supports.

One gap in today's test: "saying something false" isn't checked by either case. Adding it means giving the judge the file report so it can compare. If you agree with this list, I can turn it into the test once the other session's edits to `run_prompt_tests.py` are in.
Do you know how to write a good judging question now?

Better than I did, yes, but I haven't proven it: the only question I've tested was the bad one, and my reading of the replies was wrong too.

**What I got wrong:** I started from a rule ("leave it to the card") and asked whether the reply obeyed it. That measures obedience.

**How I'd write one now:**
1. **Start from what the person needs at that moment.** For example, someone who asked for a file to be opened needs to know it opened and what comes next.
2. **Only test what would actually hurt them if missing.** If I can't name the harm, it's not a pass-or-fail item.
3. **Let different good replies pass.** Don't require particular content or wording unless the case is about that.
4. **Write it the way you'd ask a person, with "yes" meaning pass.** One plain sentence, no exception lists. If it needs exceptions, it's probably aimed at the wrong thing.
5. **Leave counting to code.** The one-question check doesn't need a judge.
6. **Give the judge what it needs.** It can't call a claim false without seeing the file report.
7. **Test the question before trusting it.** Try it on replies it wasn't written from, including bad ones, since a question that passes everything proves nothing. Then read the verdicts myself and bring you any I'm unsure of.

**For these two cases, that would give:**
- `model-opened-unnamed`: "Does this message tell the person something true and useful about the object they just imported, or ask what it's for, and make clear what they can do next?"
- `model-opened-by-tool`: "Does this message tell the person the file they asked for was opened, say what the object is or ask what it's for, and make clear what they can do next?"

"True" only works if the judge also sees the file report, and "useful" is still a judgement call. I'd expect these to pass all ten replies, but that wouldn't tell us much until they've also been tried on bad replies, like one that gets the file's details wrong. They're untested so far.

All of this goes to the judge along with the file report:

> The assistant could also see a picture of the object, which you cannot, so accept what it says the object is or looks like. Check its other facts against the report.

Then, for each case:
- `model-opened-unnamed`: "Does this message tell the person something true and useful about the object they just imported, or ask what it's for, and make clear what they can do next?"
- `model-opened-by-tool`: "Does this message tell the person the file they asked for was opened, say what the object is or ask what it's for, and make clear what they can do next?"

**The first attempt got 7 wrong.** The judge failed all five real bunny replies and my two good bunny replies, because it can't see the picture and so treated "Stanford bunny" as made up. Telling it about the picture fixed all seven. Without that test, I'd have added a question that failed good replies.

**Results of the second attempt:**

| Reply | Should | Did |
|---|---|---|
| 10 real replies from Opus, including the six the word limit failed | pass | all passed |
| Very short good replies (one per case) | pass | passed |
| Long good reply, about 100 words, with support and size advice | pass | passed |
| Bunny: says it's broken and 400 mm | fail | failed |
| Bunny: only "The file was imported." | fail | failed |
| Bunny: describes it, but gives no next step | fail | failed |

| Cube: "Opened it. What should we do next?" | fail | failed |

I also read the judge's reason for each verdict in the second attempt, as far as my display cut-off allowed, and the ones I could see made sense.

**What this doesn't cover:**
- **Wrong object:** because the judge accepts whatever the reply says the object is, calling the bunny a teapot would pass. Catching that needs a judge that can see the picture.
- **Rambling:** with the word limit gone, nothing catches a very long message. I only tried one of about 100 words, and I never asked the judge about length.

Yes. You wanted the first message kept short, and without a check, nothing in the test would catch a long one. The problem was the check being too tight, not having one.

I see two ways to do it:

1. **A loose word limit, around 150.** Every reply so far was under 120 words, so none of them would fail, but a message that really rambles would. It's simple and gives the same answer every time, but it can't tell useful length from padding.

But it's a matter of opinion, so verdicts may vary, and it could fail the replies with setup comments you said were fine.
